In July 1518, a woman stepped into a street in Strasbourg and started to dance.
She did not stop for days.
Within a week, thirty-four more people had joined her.
Within a month, there were hundreds.
They danced until their feet bled. They did not eat, they did not rest, and they could not stop.
The doctors had an answer. They said it was caused by hot blood.
The city opened its guildhalls, built a wooden stage, and hired musicians to keep everyone moving.
Of course, it only got worse.
Some people reportedly danced themselves to death.
At last, the city banned music, tore down the stage, and sent the dancers to a shrine in the mountains.
They were given red shoes and wooden crosses, and told to pray.
Nobody knows why. Maybe it was poisoned bread. Maybe it was mass hysteria.
Either way, the city's first answer to a dancing plague was to throw a dance party.
